slides.title: SECTION 01: INTRODUCTION
slides.html:
SECTION 01: INTRODUCTION

What is a Database?

Why modern web applications cannot survive on text files or memory alone

FUNDAMENTALS

The File System Problem

Storing app data in JSON or text files fails at scale. Concurrent writes cause data corruption, searches require reading entire files into RAM, and there are no transaction safety guarantees.

The Database Solution

A Database Management System (DBMS) is specialized software engineered to store, organize, index, secure, and retrieve massive volumes of data with sub-millisecond latency and ACID reliability.

Core Responsibilities

Data persistence across server restarts, concurrency control for thousands of simultaneous users, relational integrity enforcement, authentication, and structured query optimization.

Key Takeaway: A database is not just a hard drive folder; it is a high-speed multi-threaded transaction engine engineered to protect data integrity at all times.

slides.title: SECTION 01: INTRODUCTION
slides.html:
SECTION 01: INTRODUCTION

SQL vs NoSQL: Why PostgreSQL?

Relational rigor meets modern document flexibility

INDUSTRY CHOICE

SQL (Relational)

Structured schemas, strict data types, relational joins, foreign keys, and ACID transactions. Ideal for applications with interconnected data, financial records, and clear entities.

NoSQL (Document)

Schema-less JSON documents. Flexible for rapid prototyping, but complex joins must be manually handled in application code and data duplication is common.

Why PostgreSQL Won

PostgreSQL delivers the best of both worlds: rock-solid relational ACID compliance combined with native high-performance JSONB document querying and indexing.

Feature Traditional SQL (MySQL) NoSQL (MongoDB) PostgreSQL
Relational Joins & Foreign Keys Yes Limited ($lookup) Advanced & Optimized
Semi-Structured JSON / Documents Basic JSON text Native BSON Native JSONB (Binary + GIN Index)
Extensibility Limited Custom plugins PostGIS, pgvector, Full-Text

slides.title: SECTION 02: DATABASE FUNDAMENTALS
slides.html:
SECTION 02: DATABASE FUNDAMENTALS

Database Mental Model & Hierarchy

Understanding the organizational layers from server to record

ARCHITECTURE

1. Server Cluster

The PostgreSQL service managing storage, connections, background worker processes, and memory buffers.

2. Database & Schema

A database is an isolated namespace containing schemas (default 'public'). Schemas group related tables, views, and functions.

3. Table, Column & Row

Tables represent entities. Columns define attributes with strict data types. Rows (records) store individual instances of data.

Operating System
↓
PostgreSQL Server (Port 5432)
↓
Database (myapp)
↓
Schema (public)
↓
Tables (users, posts, comments)

slides.title: SECTION 02: DATABASE FUNDAMENTALS
slides.html:
SECTION 02: DATABASE FUNDAMENTALS

Relational Architecture in Action

Visualizing connected entities: Users, Posts, and Comments

ERD VISUAL

Entities do not live in isolation. Foreign keys establish mathematically sound references between rows, eliminating duplicate data and preserving structural integrity.

table: users
id (PK) | name | email --------+-------+------------------ 1 | Dara | dara@test.com 2 | Lina | lina@test.com
table: posts
id (PK) | user_id (FK) | title --------+--------------+------------------ 101 | 1 | Intro to Postgres 102 | 1 | Serverless Neon 103 | 2 | Next.js Data Flow
table: comments
id (PK) | post_id (FK) | comment --------+--------------+------------------ 501 | 101 | Great article! 502 | 101 | Very clear tips. 503 | 103 | Thanks for this!
Relational Linkage: posts.user_id points to users.id. If Dara updates his name, every post Dara authored immediately reflects his updated name without data duplication.

SECTION 03: LOCAL INSTALLATION

Installing PostgreSQL Locally

Setting up the server environment on Linux / Ubuntu

UBUNTU / DEBIAN

Package Installation

Install the PostgreSQL server engine along with the postgresql-contrib package containing valuable extensions and utilities.

System User & Port

The package installer creates a dedicated Linux system user named 'postgres' and configures the daemon to listen on default TCP port 5432.

bash — installation commands
$sudo apt update Hit:1 http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu jammy InRelease $sudo apt install -y postgresql postgresql-contrib Setting up postgresql-client-16... Setting up postgresql-16... Creating new PostgreSQL cluster 16/main ... Ver Cluster Port Status Owner Data directory 16 main 5432 online postgres /var/lib/postgresql/16/main

slides.title: SECTION 03: LOCAL INSTALLATION
slides.html:
SECTION 03: LOCAL INSTALLATION

PostgreSQL Service Management

Controlling the background systemd daemon

SYSTEMD
bash — systemctl commands
$sudo systemctl status postgresql ● postgresql.service - PostgreSQL RDBMS Loaded: loaded (/lib/systemd/system/postgresql.service; enabled) Active: active (exited) since Mon 2026-10-19 14:00:00 UTC $sudo systemctl start postgresql $sudo systemctl enable postgresql

Service Status Check

Verify that the PostgreSQL engine is active, running, and listening for incoming client connections.

Starting & Boot Enable

Start the service immediately and enable systemd auto-restart on operating system reboots.

slides.title: SECTION 04: PSQL CLI
slides.html:
SECTION 04: PSQL CLI

The psql Interactive Terminal

Connecting to the database engine from your command line

TERMINAL CLI

What is psql?

psql is the official PostgreSQL interactive terminal program. It allows you to run SQL queries, inspect database schemas, manage roles, and execute administrative meta-commands.

The postgres Superuser

By default, PostgreSQL uses peer authentication on Linux. Running psql as the postgres user connects you directly to the administrative console.

bash — connecting as postgres
$sudo -u postgres psql psql (16.2) Type "help" for help. postgres=#

slides.title: SECTION 04: PSQL CLI
slides.html:
SECTION 04: PSQL CLI

psql Connection Parameters

Deconstructing connection flags: -h, -p, -U, -d

FLAGS & URI
Flag Parameter Default Description
-h Hostname / Host IP Local UNIX socket Server IP address or hostname (e.g., localhost or remote Neon host)
-p Port 5432 TCP port where PostgreSQL is listening
-U Username Current OS user Database role / user name to authenticate as
-d Database name Same as username Target database to connect to
bash — connection examples
$psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U postgres -d myapp $psql "postgresql://postgres:secret@localhost:5432/myapp?sslmode=disable"

slides.title: SECTION 05: IMPORTANT PSQL COMMANDS
slides.html:
SECTION 05: IMPORTANT PSQL COMMANDS

Essential psql Meta-Commands

Navigating databases and schemas without writing long SQL queries

META-COMMANDS
Command Action
\lList all databases in the server cluster
\c dbnameConnect / switch to target database
\dtList all tables in the current schema
\d table_nameDescribe table structure, columns, types, indexes
\duList all users / roles and their attributes
\dnList all schemas in current database
\qQuit / exit psql terminal session
Notice: Meta-commands begin with a backslash \ and do NOT require a trailing semicolon ;. SQL queries on the other hand MUST end with a semicolon.
psql session
postgres=# \c myapp You are now connected to database "myapp" as user "postgres". myapp=# \dt List of relations Schema | Name | Type | Owner -------+-------+-------+------- public | users | table | postgres (1 row)

slides.title: SECTION 05: IMPORTANT PSQL COMMANDS
slides.html:
SECTION 05: IMPORTANT PSQL COMMANDS

System & Environment Inspection

Checking database version, active database, and query timing

QUERIES
psql — server queries
myapp=# SELECT version(); version --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- PostgreSQL 16.2 (Ubuntu 16.2-1.pgdg22.04+1) on x86_64-pc-linux-gnu, compiled by gcc (Ubuntu 11.4.0) (1 row) myapp=# SELECT current_database(); current_database ------------------ myapp (1 row)

Server Identification

Inspect the PostgreSQL version and current connected database name to ensure you are operating in the intended environment.

Session Enhancements

Enable `\timing` to measure exact query execution milliseconds, and `\x auto` for vertical expanded output on wide tables.

slides.title: SECTION 06: CREATE & DROP DATABASE
slides.html:
SECTION 06: CREATE & DROP DATABASE

Creating & Dropping Databases

Provisioning databases and critical production precautions

PRODUCTION SAFETY
SQL Commands
postgres=# CREATE DATABASE myapp; CREATE DATABASE postgres=# \c myapp You are now connected to database "myapp" as user "postgres". myapp=# DROP DATABASE myapp; DROP DATABASE
CRITICAL PRODUCTION WARNING:
NEVER run destructive database commands (such as DROP DATABASE or DROP TABLE) against production environments without verified backups and dual confirmation.

Database Isolation

Creating a new database establishes an isolated logical container with its own schemas, tables, and permissions.

slides.title: SECTION 07: SQL FUNDAMENTALS
slides.html:
SECTION 07: SQL FUNDAMENTALS

DDL: Creating Tables with Constraints

Defining solid table schemas with data integrity guarantees

DDL
SQL — CREATE TABLE users
CREATE TABLE users (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

PRIMARY KEY

Guarantees unique identification for each row. Automatically creates an underlying B-tree index and enforces NOT NULL.

NOT NULL & UNIQUE

NOT NULL rejects records without a value. UNIQUE prevents duplicate entries (e.g. prevents duplicate customer email registrations).

slides.title: SECTION 07: SQL FUNDAMENTALS
slides.html:
SECTION 07: SQL FUNDAMENTALS

DML: Inserting & Querying Records

Writing records and executing filtered SELECT queries

INSERT & SELECT
INSERT Statements
-- Insert single row and return generated ID
INSERT INTO users (name, email)
VALUES ('Dara S.', 'dara@example.com')
RETURNING id, created_at;

-- Insert multiple rows in one query
INSERT INTO users (name, email)
VALUES 
    ('Lina K.', 'lina@example.com'),
    ('Bona T.', 'bona@example.com');
SELECT Statements
-- Select specific columns (avoid SELECT *)
SELECT id, name, email
FROM users
WHERE email = 'dara@example.com';

-- Ordered query with LIMIT
SELECT id, name
FROM users
ORDER BY id DESC
LIMIT 10;

slides.title: SECTION 07: SQL FUNDAMENTALS
slides.html:
SECTION 07: SQL FUNDAMENTALS

DML: Updating & Deleting Records

Modifying data safely and the critical danger of missing WHERE clauses

WHERE CLAUSE
UPDATE & DELETE
-- Safe UPDATE with specific WHERE target
UPDATE users
SET name = 'Dara Sam'
WHERE id = 1;

-- Safe DELETE with target ID
DELETE FROM users
WHERE id = 1;
CRITICAL MISTAKE: Omitting the WHERE clause on UPDATE or DELETE executes the operation across EVERY ROW IN THE ENTIRE TABLE!

Soft Deletes Alternative

In production applications, consider soft deletes: UPDATE users SET is_deleted = TRUE, deleted_at = NOW() WHERE id = 1; to preserve audit history and prevent accidental data loss.

slides.title: SECTION 08: POSTGRESQL DATA TYPES
slides.html:
SECTION 08: POSTGRESQL DATA TYPES

Core PostgreSQL Data Types

Choosing the optimal type for storage efficiency and data precision

DATA TYPES
NUMBERS

INTEGER / BIGINT

INTEGER is 4 bytes (-2B to +2B). BIGINT is 8 bytes. Always use BIGINT for high-traffic IDs or analytics counters.

FINANCE

NUMERIC(p, s)

Exact decimal representation. Never use FLOAT or REAL for money or currency; always use NUMERIC(12, 2).

STRINGS

TEXT vs VARCHAR

In PostgreSQL, TEXT and VARCHAR have identical underlying performance. Prefer TEXT unless strict character limit enforcement is required.

LOGIC

BOOLEAN & DATE

BOOLEAN stores true/false/null. DATE stores calendar dates (YYYY-MM-DD) without times or timezones.

slides.title: SECTION 08: POSTGRESQL DATA TYPES
slides.html:
SECTION 08: POSTGRESQL DATA TYPES

Timestamps: TIMESTAMP vs TIMESTAMPTZ

Why you should almost always use TIMESTAMPTZ in modern web apps

TIMEZONE SAFETY

TIMESTAMP (Without Time Zone)

Stores naive local time without any timezone offset. Leads to severe bugs when servers, databases, and users reside in different timezones.

TIMESTAMP '2026-10-19 14:00:00' -- Ambiguous: Is this UTC? EST? ICT (Phnom Penh)?

TIMESTAMPTZ (With Time Zone)

Internally converts and stores the timestamp in UTC. When queried, PostgreSQL formats the output based on the client session timezone.

TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-10-19 14:00:00+07' -- Stored internally as UTC: 2026-10-19 07:00:00 UTC
Golden Production Rule: Always declare timestamp columns as TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(). Your database remains strictly normalized in UTC across all global deployments.

slides.title: SECTION 08: POSTGRESQL DATA TYPES
slides.html:
SECTION 08: POSTGRESQL DATA TYPES

JSONB: Semi-Structured Power

Storing, indexing, and querying JSON inside relational tables

JSONB
SQL — Querying JSONB
-- Create table with JSONB column
CREATE TABLE user_settings (
    user_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    metadata JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
);

-- Extract as JSON object (->) vs TEXT (->>)
SELECT 
    metadata->'theme' as theme_json,
    metadata->>'theme' as theme_text
FROM user_settings
WHERE metadata->>'newsletter' = 'true';

JSON vs JSONB

JSON stores raw text. JSONB parses JSON into a decomposed binary format that supports fast indexing, fast key lookups, and rich operators.

GIN Indexing on JSONB

You can build GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) on JSONB columns: CREATE INDEX idx_meta ON user_settings USING GIN (metadata); for blazing-fast document lookups.

slides.title: SECTION 09: PRIMARY KEYS & UUID
slides.html:
SECTION 09: PRIMARY KEYS & UUID

Primary Keys: BIGSERIAL vs UUID

Comparing auto-incrementing sequential integers with distributed UUIDs

PRIMARY KEYS

BIGSERIAL (Auto-Increment Integer)

Fast, 8-byte compact storage, natural ordering. Downside: URLs expose sequential IDs (`/users/1`, `/users/2`), allowing ID enumeration attacks.

id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY

UUID (Universally Unique Identifier)

128-bit globally unique identifier. Can be generated on the client or server without coordinating with the database. Impossible to guess.

id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()
Criteria BIGSERIAL UUID
Storage Size8 bytes16 bytes
URL Enumeration AttackVulnerable (/orders/42)Secure (impossible to guess)
Client-Side GenerationNo (must ask database)Yes (generate before insert)
Index Insert PerformanceHigh (sequential append)Moderate (random B-tree page splits)

slides.title: SECTION 09: PRIMARY KEYS & UUID
slides.html:
SECTION 09: PRIMARY KEYS & UUID

Generating UUIDs & Tradeoffs

Using gen_random_uuid() and understanding B-Tree page fragmentation

gen_random_uuid()
SQL — Native UUID Generation
-- PostgreSQL 13+ built-in function
SELECT gen_random_uuid();
-- Output: c9a646d3-9c61-4cd7-bf53-73d8f7634f19

-- Creating table with UUID primary key
CREATE TABLE projects (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

gen_random_uuid()

PostgreSQL 13+ includes `gen_random_uuid()` natively without requiring the `pgcrypto` extension. Generates cryptographically secure UUIDv4.

UUID Performance Tradeoff

Random UUIDv4 values cause random index insertions, leading to B-Tree page splits and higher write amplification compared to sequential integers.

slides.title: SECTION 10: RELATIONSHIPS
slides.html:
SECTION 10: RELATIONSHIPS

Database Relationships & Cardinality

Modeling 1-to-1, 1-to-Many, and Many-to-Many associations

CARDINALITY

One-to-One (1:1)

One user has exactly one profile. Enforced with a UNIQUE foreign key.

users (id) ← (user_id UNIQUE) profiles

One-to-Many (1:N)

One user authors many posts. Standard foreign key on the posts table.

users (id) ← (user_id) posts

Many-to-Many (N:M)

Posts have many tags; tags belong to many posts. Resolved via a junction table.

posts (id) ← post_tags → tags (id)

slides.title: SECTION 10: RELATIONSHIPS
slides.html:
SECTION 10: RELATIONSHIPS

Foreign Keys & Referential Integrity

Enforcing relational constraints with ON DELETE rules

FOREIGN KEYS
SQL — Foreign Key Definition
CREATE TABLE posts (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    -- Cascading foreign key definition
    user_id BIGINT NOT NULL 
        REFERENCES users(id) 
        ON DELETE CASCADE
);
ActionBehavior on Parent Delete
CASCADEAutomatically deletes all child rows when the parent is deleted
SET NULLSets child foreign key to NULL (requires column to be nullable)
RESTRICTPrevents deleting parent while child rows exist (default safe behavior)

slides.title: SECTION 11: SQL JOINS
slides.html:
SECTION 11: SQL JOINS

Visualizing SQL Joins

Combining data across multiple tables in a single query

JOINS

INNER JOIN

A ∩ B

Returns only rows where matching values exist in both tables.

LEFT JOIN

A + (A ∩ B)

Returns all rows from left table, plus matched records from right.

RIGHT JOIN

(A ∩ B) + B

Returns all rows from right table, plus matched from left.

FULL OUTER

A ∪ B

Returns all rows whenever a match exists in either table.

slides.title: SECTION 11: SQL JOINS
slides.html:
SECTION 11: SQL JOINS

Practical Multi-Table Queries

Fetching users, their posts, and counting comments with GROUP BY

PRACTICAL SQL
SQL — Joining Users, Posts & Comment Counts
SELECT 
    users.id AS user_id,
    users.name AS author_name,
    posts.title AS post_title,
    COUNT(comments.id) AS comment_count
FROM users
INNER JOIN posts ON posts.user_id = users.id
LEFT JOIN comments ON comments.post_id = posts.id
GROUP BY users.id, users.name, posts.id, posts.title
ORDER BY comment_count DESC;

slides.title: SECTION 12: INDEXES
slides.html:
SECTION 12: INDEXES

What is a Database Index?

Speeding up query reads with B-Tree data structures

INDEXING
SQL — Creating Indexes
-- Single column index
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email 
ON users(email);

-- Composite index (multi-column)
CREATE INDEX idx_tasks_project_status 
ON tasks(project_id, status);

The B-Tree Index

Without an index, finding a user by email requires scanning every single row in the table (Sequential Scan, O(N)). An index provides an O(log N) lookup path.

Indexes Are Not Free

Indexes consume disk space and add write overhead. Every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE must also update the corresponding index trees.

slides.title: SECTION 12: INDEXES
slides.html:
SECTION 12: INDEXES

EXPLAIN & EXPLAIN ANALYZE

Measuring query planning and identifying execution bottlenecks

QUERY PLAN
EXPLAIN ANALYZE Output
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'dara@test.com'; Index Scan using idx_users_email on users (cost=0.29..8.30 rows=1 width=72) (actual time=0.038..0.040 rows=1 loops=1) Index Cond: (email = 'dara@test.com'::text) Planning Time: 0.124 ms Execution Time: 0.065 ms

Seq Scan vs Index Scan

Look for 'Seq Scan' on large tables as an indicator that a missing index is forcing PostgreSQL to read all table pages from disk.

Cost & Actual Milliseconds

Cost shows PostgreSQL query planner estimates. Actual time shows real stopwatch milliseconds measured during real execution.

slides.title: SECTION 13: TRANSACTIONS & ACID
slides.html:
SECTION 13: TRANSACTIONS & ACID

Transactions & ACID Guarantees

The four pillars of reliable, enterprise-grade data management

ACID
A

Atomicity

All operations in a transaction succeed, or all fail together. Never half-written data.

C

Consistency

Constraints (unique, foreign keys, types) are strictly enforced before committing.

I

Isolation

Concurrent transactions do not see intermediate, uncommitted modifications.

D

Durability

Committed records are permanently written to Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) on disk.

slides.title: SECTION 13: TRANSACTIONS & ACID
slides.html:
SECTION 13: TRANSACTIONS & ACID

Transaction Workflow in Action

BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK in banking and payment processing

BANK TRANSFER
SQL — Bank Transfer Transaction
BEGIN;

-- 1. Deduct from Alice
UPDATE accounts 
SET balance = balance - 100 
WHERE id = 'alice-123';

-- 2. Add to Bob
UPDATE accounts 
SET balance = balance + 100 
WHERE id = 'bob-456';

-- Commit changes permanently
COMMIT;

-- Or abort on any failure:
-- ROLLBACK;
Transferring $100 between two bank accounts requires deducting from Account A and adding to Account B. If the server crashes midway, a transaction guarantees no money vanishes.

slides.title: SECTION 14: DATABASE DESIGN
slides.html:
SECTION 14: DATABASE DESIGN

Database Normalization (1NF to 3NF)

Eliminating redundancy while keeping queries clean and maintainable

SCHEMA DESIGN

BAD DATABASE (Denormalized)

users ├─ id: 1 ├─ name: "Dara" └─ posts: "Post 1, Post 2, Post 3" <-- Comma list!

Cannot index individual posts, cannot join on author, cannot maintain referential integrity.

GOOD DATABASE (Normalized)

users (id, name, email) ↓ (1:N via user_id) posts (id, user_id, title) ↓ (1:N via post_id) comments (id, post_id, comment)

Clean, queryable, indexable, cascade-safe.

slides.title: SECTION 14: DATABASE DESIGN
slides.html:
SECTION 14: DATABASE DESIGN

Production Schema Conventions

Clean naming rules, audit fields, and column constraints

BEST PRACTICES

Naming Rules

Use lowercase snake_case. Use plural table names (users, projects) and singular foreign keys (user_id).

Audit Columns

Always add created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW() and updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW().

Explicit Constraints

Prefer NOT NULL whenever a value is required. Always add explicit foreign keys with ON DELETE policies.

slides.title: SECTION 15: MIGRATIONS
slides.html:
SECTION 15: MIGRATIONS

What are Database Migrations?

Version-controlling schema evolution across teams and environments

MIGRATIONS
0001_create_users_table.sql
↓
0002_create_projects_table.sql
↓
0003_add_avatar_to_users.sql
↓
Production Database Schema (Synced)

Why Migrations Matter

Manually executing SQL schema commands in production leads to schema drift, forgotten changes, broken deployments, and untracked alterations.

Version Pipeline

Migrations are ordered script files committed to Git. A tracking table records which migrations have run on each environment.

slides.title: SECTION 15: MIGRATIONS
slides.html:
SECTION 15: MIGRATIONS

Writing Safe Production Migrations

Executing ALTER TABLE without locking tables or breaking production

ALTER TABLE
SQL — Adding Column Safely
-- Safe: Adding nullable column or column with DEFAULT
ALTER TABLE users 
ADD COLUMN avatar_url TEXT;

-- Safe: Adding column with default (PG 11+)
ALTER TABLE users 
ADD COLUMN role TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'member';

Backwards Compatibility

Never rename or delete a column while existing application versions are running. Deploy in phases: add column -> deploy app -> migrate data -> remove old column.

Never add a NOT NULL column without a DEFAULT on a table with existing rows, as PostgreSQL will reject the migration immediately.

slides.title: SECTION 16: BACKUPS & RESTORE
slides.html:
SECTION 16: BACKUPS & RESTORE

PostgreSQL Backups: pg_dump & Restore

Creating logical SQL dumps and restoring them with psql

pg_dump
bash — dump & restore
# Backup database to SQL file pg_dump -U postgres -d myapp > backup.sql # Restore database from SQL file psql -U postgres -d myapp < backup.sql # Compressed custom format (.dump) pg_dump -U postgres -F c -d myapp > myapp.dump pg_restore -U postgres -d myapp myapp.dump

pg_dump (Logical Backup)

pg_dump extracts a consistent snapshot of the database schema and data into SQL statements or custom compressed binary format.

Restoring Data

SQL text dumps are restored using standard `psql myapp < backup.sql`. Custom directory or compressed dumps use `pg_restore`.

slides.title: SECTION 16: BACKUPS & RESTORE
slides.html:
SECTION 16: BACKUPS & RESTORE

Disaster Recovery Best Practices

Why an untested backup cannot be trusted in production

DISASTER RECOVERY
Core Engineering Rule: A backup that has never been restored is not fully trusted. You do not have a backup plan until you have verified your restore procedure.

Automated & Scheduled

Schedule automated daily backups and store them in geographically separate object storage (e.g., S3/Cloud Storage) with retention policies.

Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)

Modern cloud systems like Neon continuously stream WAL logs, allowing you to restore the database to any specific second in the past.

Restore Drills

Regularly spin up a staging database from your latest backup to verify recovery time and data integrity.

slides.title: SECTION 17: USERS & PERMISSIONS
slides.html:
SECTION 17: USERS & PERMISSIONS

PostgreSQL Roles & Permissions

Enforcing the principle of least privilege in production

SECURITY
SQL — Least Privilege User Creation
-- 1. Create dedicated application user
CREATE USER app_user WITH PASSWORD 'StrongSecretPassword123!';

-- 2. Grant connection rights
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE myapp TO app_user;

-- 3. Grant table DML permissions only
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE 
ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO app_user;
Never Use Superuser in Applications: If your web app uses the postgres superuser, an attacker exploiting SQL injection can read all databases, drop tables, or even execute arbitrary server commands.

slides.title: SECTION 18: WHAT IS NEON?
slides.html:
SECTION 18: WHAT IS NEON?

Neon: Serverless PostgreSQL Platform

Separating compute from storage for modern cloud development

NEON SERVERLESS

What is Neon?

Neon is a serverless, multi-tenant PostgreSQL platform that re-architects Postgres by splitting monolithic database compute from cloud storage.

100% Postgres Compatible

Neon runs standard 100% open-source PostgreSQL. All your queries, types, extensions, and ORM tools work with zero code modifications.

Zero Maintenance

No operating system patches, no manual disk resizing, no replication configuration. Neon handles the underlying cloud infrastructure automatically.

Next.js Web App
→
Neon Compute (Stateless Postgres)
→
Neon Pageservers (Cloud Storage & WAL)

slides.title: SECTION 18: WHAT IS NEON?
slides.html:
SECTION 18: WHAT IS NEON?

Traditional Postgres vs Neon Architecture

Monolithic local disk vs cloud storage pageservers & distributed WAL

ARCHITECTURE COMPARISON

Traditional PostgreSQL

Compute and disk are tightly coupled to a single virtual machine. Upgrades, scaling, and resizing require stopping the server or complex replication.

[ Application ] ↓ [ Single Server VM ] ├─ CPU / RAM (Compute) └─ Attached Hard Disk (Storage)

Neon Cloud Architecture

Instant Branching

slides.title: SECTION 25: DRIZZLE + NEON

SECTION 25: DRIZZLE + NEON

Drizzle ORM Schema with Neon

Defining type-safe tables in pure TypeScript

DRIZZLE ORM
schema.ts (Drizzle Definition)
import { pgTable, serial, text, timestamp, uuid } from 'drizzle-orm/pg-core';

export const users = pgTable('users', {
  id: uuid('id').defaultRandom().primaryKey(),
  name: text('name').notNull(),
  email: text('email').notNull().unique(),
  createdAt: timestamp('created_at', { withTimezone: true }).defaultNow().notNull()
});

export const posts = pgTable('posts', {
  id: serial('id').primaryKey(),
  title: text('title').notNull(),
  authorId: uuid('author_id').references(() => users.id, { onDelete: 'cascade' }).notNull()
});

import { neon } from '@neondatabase/serverless';
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/neon-http';
import { users } from './schema';

const sql = neon(process.env.DATABASE_URL!);
export const db = drizzle(sql);

// Inside Next.js App Router page.tsx
export default async function UsersPage() {
  const allUsers = await db.select().from(users);
  return (
    <div>

    </div>

slides.title: SECTION 27: CONNECTION POOLING
slides.html:
SECTION 27: CONNECTION POOLING

The Serverless Connection Problem

Why 500 lambda invocations can crash a traditional database

CONNECTION CRASH
Problem: Direct Serverless Connections
500 Serverless Functions (Vercel Lambdas) ↓ 500 separate open TCP connections! PostgreSQL Server (max_connections = 100) ↓ FATAL: sorry, too many clients already! 500 Server Error (App Outage!)

Stateless Function Concurrency

Serverless functions spin up independently on demand. When traffic surges, 500 simultaneous instances open 500 separate PostgreSQL connections.

Postgres Connection Cost

Each direct PostgreSQL connection forks a dedicated backend operating system process consuming ~10MB RAM. The server quickly runs out of memory and rejects connections.

slides.title: SECTION 27: CONNECTION POOLING
slides.html:
SECTION 27: CONNECTION POOLING

Neon Connection Pooling (PgBouncer)

Scaling to 10,000+ serverless connections seamlessly

PgBouncer POOLER
Solution: Neon Pooled Architecture
10,000 Serverless Requests ↓ Neon PgBouncer Connection Pooler (-pooler) ↓ Multiplexed into 10 persistent connections Neon PostgreSQL Compute Engine ↓ 100% Uptime • Zero Connection Exhaustion!

How to Use Neon Pooling

Simply use the pooled connection string provided in your Neon console (it appends -pooler to your host endpoint name).

Always connect your Next.js application using the Neon pooled connection string in production.

slides.title: SECTION 29: DATABASE SECURITY
slides.html:
SECTION 29: DATABASE SECURITY

Preventing SQL Injection Attacks

The critical difference between dangerous string concatenation and parameterized queries

SQL INJECTION
BAD: Vulnerable String Interpolation
// FATAL VULNERABILITY!
const query = `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${userEmail}'`;
// If user inputs: ' OR 1=1; DROP TABLE users; --
// Your entire database is destroyed!
GOOD: Parameterized Query ($1, $2)
// 100% SECURE: Engine treats input strictly as data
await sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ${userEmail}`;
// Or in psql / pg:
// SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1;

slides.title: SECTION 29: DATABASE SECURITY
slides.html:
SECTION 29: DATABASE SECURITY

Passwords, TLS/SSL & Access Control

Comprehensive security guidelines for production database deployments

ENCRYPTION & AUTH

Password Hashing

NEVER store plaintext passwords. Always hash using Argon2id or bcrypt with appropriate salt rounds before inserting into the database.

TLS / SSL Encryption

Enforce `sslmode=require` to ensure all query traffic between your web application and Neon is encrypted with modern TLS.

IP Allowlisting

On production databases, restrict network access to known CIDR IP blocks or your cloud provider VPC peering tunnel.

slides.title: SECTION 30: PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION
slides.html:
SECTION 30: PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION

Database Performance Optimization Checklist

Proven engineering practices for high-throughput, low-latency applications

CHECKLIST
01

Index Foreign Keys

PostgreSQL does NOT automatically index foreign key columns. Always index them manually.

02

Avoid SELECT *

Select only the specific columns needed by the view. Reduces RAM, serialization, and network I/O.

03

Eliminate N+1 Queries

Fetch related records using SQL Joins or batch queries (e.g., WHERE id IN (...)) instead of looping queries.

04

Enable Pooling

Use Neon PgBouncer pooled connection endpoints to prevent connection exhaustion in serverless runtimes.

slides.title: SECTION 30: PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION
slides.html:
SECTION 30: PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION

Debugging Slow Queries with EXPLAIN ANALYZE

Step-by-step diagnostic workflow for slow database calls

DIAGNOSTICS
1. Application logs alert: Query took 1,200ms
↓
2. Run in psql: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) [Your Query];
↓
3. Identify Bottleneck: Seq Scan on orders (Rows=2,000,000, Disk Reads=45,000)
↓
4. Solution: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);
↓
5. Re-run Query: Index Scan executes in 1.2ms (1000x speedup!)

slides.title: SECTION 31: SEARCH & PAGINATION
slides.html:
SECTION 31: SEARCH & PAGINATION

Pagination: The LIMIT / OFFSET Problem

Why OFFSET 100000 degrades severely on large production tables

OFFSET CLIFF
Slow OFFSET Query
-- Page 5000:
SELECT id, title, created_at
FROM tasks
ORDER BY id ASC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;

The OFFSET Penalty

`LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000` requires PostgreSQL to read, sort, and discard 100,000 rows before returning the 20 requested records, creating high CPU and I/O load.

Data Drift

If new rows are inserted while users paginate, rows shift across page boundaries, resulting in users seeing duplicate items.

slides.title: SECTION 31: SEARCH & PAGINATION
slides.html:
SECTION 31: SEARCH & PAGINATION

Keyset (Cursor-Based) Pagination

Consistent O(1) performance regardless of dataset depth

CURSOR O(1)
Keyset / Cursor Query
-- Next page starts immediately after last seen ID:
SELECT id, title, created_at
FROM tasks
WHERE id > 100020
ORDER BY id ASC
LIMIT 20;

How Keyset Pagination Works

Query records where the primary key is greater than the last seen ID: `WHERE id > $last_id ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT 20`. Jumps directly via B-tree index seek.

Execution time on 10,000,000 rows remains identical on Page 1 as on Page 100,000 (~0.1ms).

TaskFlow manages teams, projects, tasks, and comments. Four interconnected relational tables establish clear ownership, assignment, and discussion threads.

slides.title: SECTION 33: BUILD TASKFLOW STEP-BY-STEP
slides.html:
SECTION 33: BUILD TASKFLOW STEP-BY-STEP

TaskFlow DDL: Tables & Custom Types

Creating users, projects, and custom ENUM types

DDL PART 1
SQL — DDL: Users, ENUM & Projects
-- 1. Create custom ENUM for task status
CREATE TYPE task_status AS ENUM ('todo', 'in_progress', 'review', 'done');

-- 2. Create users table
CREATE TABLE users (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- 3. Create projects table
CREATE TABLE projects (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    description TEXT,
    owner_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

slides.title: SECTION 33: BUILD TASKFLOW STEP-BY-STEP
slides.html:
SECTION 33: BUILD TASKFLOW STEP-BY-STEP

TaskFlow DDL: Tasks & Comments Schema

Implementing cascading foreign keys and performance indexes

DDL PART 2
SQL — DDL: Tasks & Comments with Indexes
-- 4. Create tasks table
CREATE TABLE tasks (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    project_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    assigned_to UUID REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    status task_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'todo',
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- 5. Create comments table
CREATE TABLE comments (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    task_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tasks(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    author_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    body TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- 6. Add performance indexes on foreign keys
CREATE INDEX idx_tasks_project ON tasks(project_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_tasks_assigned ON tasks(assigned_to);
CREATE INDEX idx_comments_task ON comments(task_id);

FROM tasks
LEFT JOIN users ON users.id = tasks.assigned_to

slides.title: SECTION 37: 12 COMMON DATABASE MISTAKES
slides.html:
SECTION 37: 12 COMMON DATABASE MISTAKES

Top 12 Beginner & Production Mistakes

Critical anti-patterns to avoid in professional database management

ANTI-PATTERNS
1. Using Superuser in App

Never connect your app as postgres. Use a dedicated restricted user.

2. Exposing DATABASE_URL

Never prefix with NEXT_PUBLIC_ in your Next.js environment variables.

3. Forgetting Foreign Key Indexes

PostgreSQL does not auto-index FKs; always create them manually.

4. Using TIMESTAMP without TZ

Always use TIMESTAMPTZ to avoid timezone calculation bugs.

5. SELECT * Everywhere

Fetches unused columns, wasting memory, CPU, and network bandwidth.

6. Raw String SQL Concatenation

Always use parameterized queries ($1, $2) to prevent SQL injection.

7. Direct Serverless Connections

Use Neon PgBouncer pooled connection strings to prevent exhaustion.

8. Unchecked UPDATE / DELETE

Forgetting WHERE updates or deletes every row in the table.

9. Untested Backups

A backup never restored is an illusion; drill your restore procedures.

10. Manual Schema Edits in Prod

Always apply schema modifications via version-controlled migrations.

11. Missing Unique Constraints

Relying solely on frontend validation results in duplicate data.

12. High OFFSET Pagination

Use keyset / cursor pagination for fast O(1) performance at scale.
